edges.description: The substituted basic domain changes where TWIST2 binds the genome.
Mutant subunits in half of TWIST2 homodimers and bHLH heterodimers either fail to occupy normal targets or occupy new ones, changing transcription of more than one downstream gene.
Aberrant TWIST2 target expression is proposed to disturb the dermal extracellular matrix.
Disturbed TWIST2-directed mesenchymal development is proposed to underlie the facial and eyelid malformations; the steps in eyelid morphogenesis are not established.
The same disturbance is proposed to produce the facial patterning defects of the mouth, nose and ears.
Disorganised dermal elastic and collagen fibres are the observed tissue correlate of lax, redundant skin; no study has tested the link directly.
Thin dermis with disordered fibres is the tissue correlate of the thin skin.
Loss of dermal fibre organisation is the tissue correlate of the excessive wrinkling and facial creases.
Atrophic skin, one of the four features in the original descriptive name, is the clinical expression of the thin, disorganised dermis.
A deficient anterior lamella everts the lid margin.
The same developmental deficiency, at its more severe end, gives microblepharon.

nodes.description:
In ChIP-seq of HeLa cells overexpressing tagged TWIST2, wild-type protein bound 630 sites with a canonical E-box consensus. Each mutant shared only a fraction of those peaks, and the two BSS alleles tested beside it (p.Glu75Ala and p.Gln77_Arg78dup) shared only 25; all mutants also bound many sites the wild-type protein did not. The lesion is therefore both a loss of normal target occupancy and a gain of new occupancy.
PROVISIONAL because this is overexpression in a non-mesenchymal cancer cell line. Binding in craniofacial or dermal mesenchyme, at endogenous expression, with the wild-type allele present, has not been measured.

nodes.description:
TWIST2 is expressed in craniofacial mesenchyme and chondrogenic precursors during embryonic development and is thought to direct development of dermal and chondrogenic tissue. Expressing the Barber-Say (p.Glu75Gln) or AMS (p.Glu75Lys) protein in zebrafish embryos produced more severe developmental defects than wild-type TWIST2 and down-regulated genes for extracellular matrix, membrane and cytoskeletal components.
PROVISIONAL: the tissue-expression premise comes from the background of the primary paper, and the transcriptome is from zebrafish embryos injected with human mRNA at the one-cell stage, which over-expresses TWIST2 globally rather than modelling a heterozygous allele in mesenchyme. No patient-cell transcriptome for a Barber-Say allele has been reported.

nodes.description:
Underdevelopment of the anterior lamella of the eyelid is a defining ophthalmic finding across the TWIST2 Glu75 disorders. In Barber-Say syndrome it presents mainly as ectropion, and less often as microblepharon; the severe end, ablepharon, characterises the allelic ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome. Surgical exploration in one patient found abnormal external and internal eyelid anatomy.
PROVISIONAL because no study has traced a Glu75 allele through eyelid morphogenesis; the link from TWIST2 to the eyelid is inferred from the phenotype and from where TWIST2 is expressed.

nodes.description: A heterozygous substitution of the conserved glutamic acid at codon 75 of TWIST2, in the basic region of the bHLH domain that contacts DNA. Glutamine (p.Glu75Gln) is the recurrent Barber-Say allele and alanine (p.Glu75Ala) the second; one proband carried an in-frame duplication of codons 77-78 (p.Gln77_Arg78dup) in the same domain. Lysine at the same residue (p.Glu75Lys) gives ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome instead, so the substituting amino acid, not only the position, sets the phenotype. In silico modelling places Glu75 facing the DNA major groove next to the first two nucleotides of the E-box, and predicts no change in global protein structure.
